Looking only at logit-level metrics, the top-1 and sequence agreement look strong and close to the quantized baseline, with KL and TV divergence both near expected ranges, though TV is slightly low. DiFR is a bit higher than the quantized comparison, and the raw-score shift of 3.2 sits between the quantized baseline (2.3) and the fine-tune backdoor and sp bias cases (3.3-3.4), which makes me want to dig into what that shift actually implies.

Checking against fine-tune backdoor specifically, the KL (0.03 vs 0.15) and top-1 (0.955 vs 0.909) numbers are far enough apart to rule it out, and TV also diverges enough (0.038 vs 0.086). Fine-tune bias is ruled out by its raw score of 10.4, and system-prompt bias is ruled out based on KL. That leaves quantization as the most likely explanation, though the raw-score shift being off by roughly nine spreads from expected is nagging at me — I wonder if this ratio naturally increases when TV is small. Overall I'll go with quantization, but with moderate confidence around 0.7.

answer.justification: Only logit-level measurements are available. They show the smallest logit change in the document. Top-1 agreement is 0.955 (quantization 0.951) and sequence agreement is 0.688 (quantization 0.688, an exact match). KL is 0.030 (quantization 0.051±0.018) and TV is 0.038 (quantization 0.051). Both system-prompt classes are ruled out: their KL is 0.24–0.30 and top-1 agreement 0.87–0.89. Fine-tune bias is ruled out by the raw-score shift: 3.2 here against its 10.4, plus its higher KL and TV (0.082). Fine-tune backdoor is the main alternative because its raw-score shift (3.3) matches 3.2 closely, better than quantization's 2.3. However, its KL (0.153), TV (0.086) and top-1 agreement (0.909) are far from what was measured. The raw-score shift is divided by TV, so a smaller TV can push the ratio up, and that one mismatch with quantization is the reason confidence is moderate rather than high. Without activation data (size ratio, onset, rank), quantization cannot be confirmed further.
